summary: Describes a protocol for carrying accounting information between a Network Access Server and a shared accounting server, which is used to record usage of network services. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Like a meter that counts how long you used the service, this tells a central server how much each person used so they can be billed.

questions: what port does radius accounting use
what is a network access server
subtitle: How a network access server reports who used what service, and for how long, to a central accounting server.

tldr.problem: Dial-in and modem pools need a central record of the service each user received, but the RADIUS protocol only covered authentication and authorization.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Access Server sends Accounting-Request packets (Start and Stop) over UDP to the accounting server, authenticated with a shared secret and an MD5-based authenticator, and gets an Accounting-Response only once the record is stored.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2139 and is an Informational memo. It has been updated by RFC 2867, RFC 5080, RFC 5997 and RFC 9765.

today: RFC 2866 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 2139. It has been updated by RFC 2867, RFC 5080, RFC 5997 and RFC 9765.

sections.title: Extending RADIUS to Accounting
sections.content:
Managing dispersed serial line and modem pools for many users takes significant administrative effort, and modem pools need careful attention to security, authorization and accounting. The best approach is a single database of users that handles authentication and the configuration of the service to deliver, such as SLIP, PPP, telnet or rlogin.

RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service, RFC 2865) covers authentication and authorization. This memo extends it to carry accounting information from the Network Access Server (NAS) to a RADIUS accounting server. The NAS is the client and the server confirms that it received the request. The server can also act as a proxy client to other kinds of accounting servers.

Three features are highlighted: the client/server model, network security through a shared secret that is never sent over the network, and an extensible protocol built from variable-length Attribute-Length-Value 3-tuples, so new attributes can be added without disturbing existing implementations.
sections.eli5: The first RADIUS decided who may come in. This part keeps score of what each visitor did, by sending short notes to a record keeper.

sections.title: Start, Stop and Retries
sections.content:
When service begins, the client generates an Accounting Start packet describing the service and the user, and the server acknowledges it. When service ends, the client sends an Accounting Stop packet describing the service delivered and, optionally, statistics such as elapsed time, input and output octets or packets. Each service delivered to a user is a session, and each session produces its own start and stop records with its own Acct-Session-Id.

The client is recommended to keep sending an Accounting-Request until it is acknowledged, using some form of backoff, and may fall back to alternate servers, either after a number of failed tries or round-robin. The RFC says retry and fallback algorithms are the topic of current research and does not specify them in detail.

The server MUST NOT send an Accounting-Response if it cannot record the packet. In a proxy arrangement, the forwarding server may log the request, add its own Proxy-State and forward it. It must not modify existing Proxy-State or Class attributes, and it may either pass retransmissions through or take responsibility for them.
sections.eli5: The desk writes a note when you arrive and when you leave. If the office does not answer, the desk keeps trying until it does.

sections.title: Packet Format and Types
sections.content:
Exactly one RADIUS Accounting packet is carried in the data field of a UDP datagram sent to destination port 1813. Replies swap the source and destination ports. Early deployments used port 1646, which conflicts with the sa-msg-port service, so 1813 is the officially assigned port.

The packet has a one-octet Code, a one-octet Identifier, a two-octet Length and a 16-octet Authenticator, followed by attributes. The codes are 4 for Accounting-Request and 5 for Accounting-Response. Length counts the whole packet, with a minimum of 20 and a maximum of 4095. Bytes beyond Length are padding and ignored, and a packet shorter than Length is silently discarded.

An Accounting-Request must carry either NAS-IP-Address or NAS-Identifier. Attributes such as User-Password, CHAP-Password, Reply-Message and State must not appear in it. The Identifier must change whenever the attributes change, and stay the same for identical retransmissions. A response copies the Identifier, and may carry no attributes at all.
sections.eli5: Each note has a small header like an envelope: what kind of note it is, a number to match it to its reply, how long it is, and a secret stamp.

sections.title: Authenticators and the Shared Secret
sections.content:
The NAS and the accounting server share a secret that is never sent over the network. In an Accounting-Request the Request Authenticator is a 16-octet MD5 hash computed over the Code, Identifier and Length, 16 zero octets, the request attributes and the shared secret. It cannot be calculated like an Access-Request authenticator, since an Accounting-Request has no User-Password.

The Response Authenticator in an Accounting-Response is an MD5 hash over the response Code, Identifier and Length, the Request Authenticator of the request being answered, the response attributes and the shared secret. Invalid responses are silently discarded. The Security Considerations section simply points to these authenticators and the shared secret.

One practical consequence: if Acct-Delay-Time is included and changes on a retransmission, the attributes change, so a new Identifier and Request Authenticator are required.
sections.eli5: The desk and the office share a secret password. They mix it into each note and each reply like a stamp that proves who sent it.

sections.title: Accounting Attributes
sections.content:
Each attribute has a one-octet type, a one-octet length and a value. Types 40 to 51 are defined here. Acct-Status-Type (40) says whether the record marks a Start, Stop, Interim-Update, Accounting-On or Accounting-Off. Acct-Session-Id (44) is a unique ID that makes it easy to match start and stop records, and every Accounting-Request must have one.

The usage counters are Acct-Input-Octets (42), Acct-Output-Octets (43), Acct-Input-Packets (47), Acct-Output-Packets (48) and Acct-Session-Time (46), all of which can appear only in records where the status is Stop. Acct-Delay-Time (41) says how many seconds the client has been trying to send the record. Acct-Terminate-Cause (49) gives one of 18 reasons a session ended, such as User Request, Lost Carrier, Idle Timeout or Session Timeout.

Acct-Authentic (45) says whether the user was authenticated by RADIUS, locally or remotely. Acct-Multi-Session-Id (50) and Acct-Link-Count (51) tie together the sessions of a multilink session, so a server can tell when it has received all the Stop records for it.
sections.eli5: Each note has labeled blanks to fill in: arrival or departure, how long, how much was used, and why the visit ended.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2139
sections.content:
This memo obsoletes RFC 2139. The change log lists: US-ASCII replaced by UTF-8, added notes on proxy operation, a rule that Framed-IP-Address should contain the actual IP address of the user, a rule that an Acct-Session-Id sent in an Access-Request must be reused in the Accounting-Request for that session, and new values for Acct-Status-Type.

It also adds an IANA Considerations section, which says the packet type codes, attribute types and attribute values are registered from the RADIUS name spaces described in RFC 2865, updates the references, and identifies text strings as a subset of strings to clarify the use of UTF-8.
sections.eli5: This is an updated rulebook. It fixes the text rules, adds notes for helpers in the middle and adds a few new options.

fields.name: Authenticator
fields.desc: 16 octets; MD5-based Request or Response Authenticator.

messages.label: Accounting-Response
messages.note: Sent only if the record was stored.

messages.label: Accounting-Request (Stop)
messages.note: Service ends; may carry time and octet counts.

items.label: Accounting-On
items.desc: Client marks the start of accounting, for example upon booting.

items.label: Accounting-Off
items.desc: Client marks the end of accounting, for example before a scheduled reboot.
